article.title: What Is Cristalino Tequila? The Filtered Añejo Explained
article.body:
What Is Cristalino Tequila? The Filtered Añejo Explained

Cristalino is aged tequila, usually añejo, that has been filtered, typically through charcoal, to remove its colour. It keeps some of the barrel's vanilla and oak but tastes lighter and smoother than an amber añejo. Drinks House 247 notes that it is a style rather than an official tequila category, so the label still states the age class.

Pour a cristalino and it looks like a blanco: perfectly clear. Taste it and you find vanilla, caramel and soft oak, the flavours of a tequila that has spent a year or more in a barrel. That contrast is the whole idea, and it has made cristalino one of the most talked-about styles in tequila.

How is cristalino made?

It starts as an aged tequila, most often an añejo, which has spent at least a year in oak. Time in the barrel gives the spirit its amber colour and its wood-derived flavours. The producer then filters the aged tequila, usually through activated charcoal, which removes the colour and some of the heavier compounds picked up from the wood. What remains is a clear spirit that still carries part of the barrel's character.

Each producer uses its own method: the type of charcoal, the number of filtrations and how long the spirit is in contact with it all change the result. Some cristalinos are made from reposado or extra añejo rather than añejo, and the label will say which.

Is cristalino an official category?

No. The official tequila categories are defined by age: blanco, joven, reposado, añejo and extra añejo. Cristalino is a style made within those categories, not a class of its own. That is why a cristalino bottle also states its age class, such as "Tequila Añejo", somewhere on the label. When comparing bottles, the age class tells you more about what went into it than the word cristalino does.

How does it compare with other tequilas?

Style Time in oak Colour Typical flavour Typical use
BlancoNone, or under two monthsClearFresh cooked agave, pepper, citrusMargaritas, Palomas, sipping
ReposadoTwo months to a yearPale goldAgave with light vanilla and oakSipping, richer cocktails
AñejoOne to three yearsAmberVanilla, caramel, dried fruit, oakSipping neat
CristalinoUsually one year or more, then filteredClearSoft vanilla and caramel, lighter oak, smooth textureChilled neat, over ice, highballs
Extra añejoOver three yearsDeep amberRich oak, spice, chocolate, dried fruitSipping slowly

Why do some tequila lovers dislike it?

The criticism is simple: filtering removes flavour as well as colour. A purist's view is that if you age a tequila for years and then strip out part of what the barrel gave it, you end up with something less characterful than either a good blanco or a good añejo. Some also feel the style leans towards sweetness and smoothness at the expense of the agave itself.

The other side of the argument is that cristalino is simply a different drink, made for people who enjoy the softness of an aged tequila but want something lighter, cleaner and easier to drink cold. Both views are fair. It comes down to what you want from the glass.

Where did cristalino come from?

Filtering aged spirits to remove colour is not new: many white rums are aged and then filtered clear. In tequila, the style took off in the 2010s. Don Julio 70, launched in 2011, is widely credited with popularising it, and since then many major tequila brands have released a cristalino of their own.

How should you serve cristalino?

  • Chilled and neat in a small glass. Its soft texture suits being served cold more than most aged tequilas.
  • Over a large ice cube, which chills it slowly without diluting it too fast.
  • In a highball with soda water or tonic and a twist of orange or grapefruit.
  • In clear, spirit-forward cocktails, where you want aged flavour without colour.

If you already enjoy añejo neat at room temperature, try a cristalino side by side with it. It is the quickest way to decide which camp you are in.

Who is it for?

Cristalino suits people who find blanco too sharp and añejo too heavy, those who like their spirits cold, and anyone exploring tequila beyond shots and Margaritas. It also makes a good gift for someone who enjoys smooth, approachable spirits. If the person you are buying for loves the bold, woody character of a traditional añejo, choose an añejo instead.

Frequently asked questions

What is cristalino tequila?

Cristalino is aged tequila, usually añejo, that has been filtered, typically through charcoal, to remove its colour. It keeps some of the barrel's vanilla and oak flavour but tastes lighter and smoother.

Is cristalino an official type of tequila?

No. The official categories are based on age, such as blanco, reposado and añejo. Cristalino is a style made within those categories, so the label still shows the age class.

Is cristalino tequila aged?

Yes. It is made from tequila aged in oak, usually for a year or more, which is then filtered clear. Some cristalinos are made from reposado or extra añejo.

How should you drink cristalino?

Chilled and neat, over a large ice cube, or in a highball with soda water or tonic. Its soft texture suits being served cold.
